summary: This document defines new DLEP Data Items and messages for credit-based flow control. Credit windows regulate when data may be sent into an associated virtual or physical queue.

plainLanguage.summary: A router wants to send lots of data to a modem, but the modem only has so much buffer space. The modem states how many bytes it can take, and the router stops sending when that amount is used up.

subtitle: How a DLEP modem hands out byte credits so a router never overruns the modem's queues.

tldr.problem: DLEP does not include any flow control, so a router can send traffic to a modem that has no buffer space for it.
tldr.mechanism: The modem advertises one credit window per flow, measured in octets, and grants more credit as it frees queue space. The router spends credits for each packet it sends and must not send when none remain. Two new messages and five new Data Items carry the credits.
tldr.outcome: Credit-based flow control is proactive, so packet loss from insufficient buffer space is less likely than with a pause mechanism. The messages and Data Items are reusable by extensions such as RFC 9894.

today: RFC 9893 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2026, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It supplies the common credit messages and Data Items that extensions such as RFC 9894 build on.

sections.title: Why DLEP Needs Credits
sections.content:
The Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) (RFC 8175) lets a router and a modem exchange link-related control information. DLEP defines a base set of mechanisms and support for possible extensions, and it defines Data Items, which are sets of information that can be reused in DLEP messaging. The DLEP specification does not include any flow identification beyond the DLEP endpoints, and it does not address flow control capability.

Various flow control techniques are theoretically possible with DLEP. For example, a credit window scheme for destination-specific flow control that provides aggregate flow control for both modems and routers has been proposed, and a mechanism called the Control-Plane-Based Pause Extension is defined in RFC 8651. The use of other flow control mechanisms at the same time as credit-based flow control is out of scope for this document.

Credit-based flow control, because it is proactive, may offer some advantages over a pause mechanism. Packet loss resulting from insufficient buffer space is less likely, since a transmitter does not send packets until the receiver has indicated that there is sufficient buffer space available.

This document defines DLEP Data Items that provide a flow control mechanism for traffic sent from a router to a modem. Flow control is provided using one or more logical credit windows, each typically supported by an associated virtual or physical queue. Credit windows may be shared or dedicated on a per-flow basis. The Data Items are structured to allow the reuse of the defined flow control with different traffic classification techniques. A router logically consumes credits for each credit window matching packet sent.

The document defines common messages, Data Items and mechanisms that are reusable, and they are expected to be required by DLEP extensions defined in other documents, such as the extension in RFC 9894. It introduces credit window flow control by defining two new DLEP messages and five new DLEP Data Items.
sections.plainLanguage: A router wants to send lots of data to a modem, but the modem only has so much room. The modem gives out permission slips so the router never sends more than fits.

sections.title: Credit Windows, Flows and Classifiers
sections.content:
Credits are managed on a per logical credit window basis, and each credit window can be thought of as corresponding to a queue within a modem. Credit windows may be shared across, or dedicated to, destinations and data plane identifiers such as DSCPs, at a granularity appropriate to a modem's implementation and its attached transmission technology. There is a direct one-to-one mapping of credit windows to flows, identified by the Flow Identifiers carried in the Traffic Classification Data Item of RFC 9892.

Modems pass to the router information on their credit windows and FIDs before a router is able to send data. Traffic Classification Identifier values and FID values are significant only to the issuing modem: there is no relationship implied by the same TID or FID value being issued by more than one modem. In addition to the traffic classification information associated with a FID, modems provide an initial credit window size and the maximum size of the logical queue associated with each credit window, the latter for informative and potential future uses.

Modems provide an initial credit window size at the time of credit window initialization, which can take place during session initiation or at any point thereafter, and also when rate information changes. An increment to a credit window size is provided in a Credit Window Grant Data Item. A router provides its own view of the credit window, known as Status, in Destination Up Response Messages and Credit Control Response Messages, and routers can also request credits using the Credit Control Message.

When a destination becomes reachable, the modem associates the appropriate traffic classification information with it through the TID to be used for traffic sent by the router to that destination, using the Credit Window Association Data Item. Traffic is mapped to a credit window by locating a matching FID inside the TID associated with the traffic's destination. Credits flow in one direction only: they are never provided by the router to the modem.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of traffic has its own credit window, measured in bytes. The router looks at the classification of each packet to find the window it must spend from.

sections.title: The Two Credit Messages
sections.content:
This document defines two new messages that support credit window flow control, the Credit Control Message and the Credit Control Response Message. Sending and receiving both message types is REQUIRED to support the mechanisms defined here. Each sender is only permitted to have one message outstanding at one time: a sender, whether modem or router, MUST NOT send a subsequent Credit Control Message until a Credit Control Response Message has been received from its peer.

Credit Control Messages are sent by modems to provide credit window increases, when the modem's transmission or local queue availability exceeds the credit window value previously provided to the router. A Credit Control Message sent by a modem MUST contain one or more Credit Window Grant Data Items, and a router receiving it MUST respond with a Credit Control Response Message. Credit Control Messages MAY also be sent by routers to request credits and provide window status; a router's message MUST contain one or more Credit Window Request Data Items and SHOULD contain a Credit Window Status Data Item corresponding to each request, and a modem receiving it MUST respond.

A Credit Control Response Message sent by a router MUST contain one or more Credit Window Status Data Items. A Credit Control Response Message sent by a modem MUST contain one or more Credit Window Grant Data Items, one for every Credit Window Request Data Item in the Credit Control Message it answers, and each grant MAY provide zero or more additional credits.

The Message Type value in the DLEP Message Header is 17 for the Credit Control Message and 18 for the Credit Control Response Message.
sections.plainLanguage: One side says "here are more credits" or "I need more credits". The other side must answer before the first can say anything new.

sections.title: The Five Data Items
sections.content:
Each Data Item has a type, a length and its fields. A wrong length makes the item corrupt, so the message cannot be reliably parsed and is ignored. Other parsing errors terminate the session with a Status Data Item indicating Invalid Data.

  • Credit Window Initialization (type 30, length 16): sent by the modem to identify a credit window by FID and give its size. It carries a 64-bit Credit Value in octets, an 8-bit Scale of 0 bytes, 1 KB, 2 MB or 3 GB, and a 24-bit Credit Window Max Size. It SHOULD appear in any Session Initialization Response that indicates support, and updates MAY go in Session Update Messages.
  • Credit Window Association (type 31, length 2): carries a TID, in every Destination Up and Destination Update Message from the modem. A TID is not used unless it is listed here.
  • Credit Window Grant (type 32, length 12): the modem adds Additional Credits, a 64-bit octet count, to the window for a FID. Zero means none are added.
  • Credit Window Status (type 33, length 12): the router reports the Current Credit Window Size, a 64-bit octet count.
  • Credit Window Request (type 34, variable length): the router lists FIDs, 2 octets each, whose windows need credits. The value 0xFFFF means all FIDs.

The Credit Value and the Additional Credits both include the MAC headers as seen on the link between the modem and router, and the Credit Window Max Size is expressed in the octet scale given by the Scale field.
sections.plainLanguage: Five kinds of Data Item are defined: set up a credit window, say which classification set a destination uses, grant credits, report the credits left, and request more credits.

sections.title: The Rules for Sending Data
sections.content:
When credit windowing is used, a router MUST NOT send data traffic to a modem for forwarding if there is no matching classifier. If a matching classifier is found, the router MUST NOT send data traffic when there are no credits available in the associated credit window. The router MUST ensure that sufficient credits are available for the current data packet before sending it. The count of octets in the packet includes MAC overhead: taking Ethernet as an example, framing, header and trailer are all included in this count. Credit windows are defined in octets, and the window is decremented by the number of sent octets.

Actual flows of traffic are mapped to credit windows using the flow identification information the modem provides in the Traffic Classification Data Item. The router uses the combination of the DLEP-identified destination and the flow information associated with a credit window in order to match traffic to specific credit windows. In some cases the Data Item allows the modem to specify a wildcard that matches any packets that do not match other Data Items. In the absence of a wildcard, a packet may match none of the Data Items, and in that case it MUST be dropped by the router.

The rules for handling each Data Item are also specified. On a Credit Window Initialization, the router checks that the FID was provided by the modem in a Traffic Classification Data Item, and SHOULD log the information if it was not; it then creates the window, or updates an existing one. If the credit value would exceed the Credit Window Max Size, the maximum becomes the window size. Updates can also reduce a window, for example after a transmission rate change on the modem; after sending such an update the modem SHOULD continue processing received packets that match the FIDs and fit within the old window, and SHOULD NOT issue additional credits for any affected FID until that window has drained below the new maximum.

On a Grant, the router increases the window by the Additional Credits, capped at the maximum. Credit windows are managed independently of the destination named in the message carrying the Data Item. For a Grant received in any message other than a Credit Control Response, the router MUST report the result in a Credit Window Status Data Item, in the Destination Up Response for a Destination Up and otherwise in a Credit Control Message.

On a Status, the modem SHOULD compare the reported size with what it expects. If the difference is more than observed data frames explain, it SHOULD send a Credit Window Initialization Data Item to reset the window; for small differences it MAY adjust later grants instead. On a Request, the modem MUST answer with Grant Data Items in a new Credit Control Message, and unknown FIDs SHOULD be logged and ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the router sends a packet, it checks that the window holds enough credits for the whole packet, including the MAC overhead. If the packet matches no classification rule at all, the router drops it.

sections.title: Management Considerations
sections.content:
Modems MAY support configuration of the number of credit windows, that is queues, to advertise to a router. Routers may have limits on the number of queues they can support, and may even have limits on supported credit window combinations; for example, per-destination queues may not be supported at all.

When credit window information provided by a modem exceeds the capabilities of a router, the router SHOULD use a subset of the provided credit windows. Alternatively, the router MAY reset the session and indicate that the extension is not supported. In either case the mismatch SHOULD be reported to the user through normal network management mechanisms such as the user interface or error logging. In all cases, if credit windows are in use, traffic for which credits are not available MUST NOT be sent to the modem by the router.

Modems also have to take into account the overhead of their attached transmission technology and map it into the credit semantics defined here. The credit window is defined to include per-frame MAC headers, and this may not match the actual overhead of the modem's transmission technology, so a direct mapping or an approximation has to be made by the modem to provide appropriate credit values.
sections.plainLanguage: If the router cannot support as many credit windows as the modem offers, it uses a subset and reports the mismatch through normal network management mechanisms.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document introduces credit window flow control mechanisms for DLEP, which expose vulnerabilities similar to existing DLEP messages. An example of a threat to which flow control might be susceptible is where a malicious actor masquerading as a DLEP peer injects a Credit Window Initialization Data Item that resizes a credit window to a value that results in a denial of service. Other possible threats are discussed in the Security Considerations section of RFC 8175 and are also applicable, though not specific, to flow control.

The transport-layer security mechanisms documented in RFC 8175, along with the latest version of BCP 195 at the time of writing, can be applied to this document. The Layer 2 security mechanisms documented in RFC 8175 can also, with some updates, be applied to the mechanisms defined here. Examples of technologies that can be deployed to secure the Layer 2 link include IEEE 802.1AE and IEEE 8802-1X.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker posing as a DLEP peer could inject a Credit Window Initialization Data Item that resizes a window so the router can never send again. The transport security mechanisms of RFC 8175 help prevent that.

viz.caption: THE PIECES OF THE CREDIT MECHANISM

items.title: Credit window
items.text: A logical queue inside the modem, holding a number of octets the router may still send.

items.title: Flow identifier
items.text: A 2-octet number from the Traffic Classification Data Item that names one flow, and so one credit window.

items.title: Traffic classification identifier
items.text: A 16-bit number the modem uses for a set of flows, and which it associates with a destination.

items.title: Credits
items.text: Counted in octets and including MAC overhead, so the window shrinks by the size of each packet sent.
